Eli Okun Politico 14 mins ago fresh drop

How SNAP could crunch the midterms

Under the political radar, the country’s food stamps program is undergoing a slow-motion transformation. The ramifications could bubble up into the midterms. Changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program from Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act are rolling out in phases, from tougher work requirements to restrictions on non-citizens. Food stamp rolls already shrank by more than 5 million people nationwide as of this summer, as the hardest-hit state, Arizona, saw an outright majority of its food stamp recipients lose benefits. The latest alteration clicked into place Oct. 1, when the share of administrative costs states and counties have to pay rose to 75% from 50%. An even bigger financial shift looms in a year, when states with high payment error rates will have to assume some benefit costs for the first time, a scenario that’s already rippling through state and local budget planning. It all adds up to a new era in federal-state relations — and in the size and nature of the welfare state. In a year when affordability worries top voters’ priority lists and grocery prices strain their wallets, Democrats think the SNAP shift gives them an opening to make Republicans pay politically after the GOP used social safety net cuts to food aid and Medicaid to help pay for last year’s tax cuts. “People are getting kicked off these programs at the very moment they’re going to the polls to vote,” House Agriculture ranking member Angie Craig (D-Minn.) said. “I sure wouldn’t want to be a Republican headed into the November ballot.” But Republicans think they have a compelling story to tell voters, trying to right-size a program that spends millions of dollars on erroneous payments. The SNAP changes align with the Trump administration’s broader push to crack down on fraud and make the government smaller or more efficient. Implementing stricter work requirements for welfare often polls well, and trying to move people toward work gets at the root causes of poverty, they argue. “The premise is simple: Let’s make sure that this program is preserved for those truly in need, and that we aren’t squandering taxpayer dollars,” a senior USDA official told Playbook in an interview. “And let’s make sure that if folks are able-bodied, they are work training or volunteering for 20 hours per week.” That doesn’t mean Republicans in competitive races are putting SNAP and Medicaid cuts front and center on the campaign trail. When they tout last year’s megalaw, new tax breaks typically lead the messaging. And 10 frontline GOP House campaigns didn’t respond to requests for interviews about how they can win on SNAP. At the state and county level, some governments are scrambling to prepare for a massive cost shift, hitting at the same time as significant Medicaid changes. The resulting bureaucratic jumble has contributed to some of the SNAP losses this year, as recipients struggled to get through overtaxed call centers, some states cut staff, and others tightened their processes. “It really sets up a change in the federal responsibility, and I view it as a slippery slope,” warned Barbara Guinn, New York’s commissioner of the Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance. Her state is staring down a possible $1 billion added burden next year, though they’re advocating for a repeal of the benefits change. “Once they implement any kind of cost shift, I think it will be easier for them to take similar actions in the future.” Whether to delay next year’s cost shift has already generated tensions over the farm bill in the Senate, where Democrats are demanding a longer postponement than Republicans’ offer of one year. Some Minnesota counties are considering significant property tax increases to pay for the extra costs, Craig said: “We’re going to be pushing hard for a two-year delay — at the request of, frankly, many of my Republican county commissioners, not just Democrats.” Conservatives see the new calculus as a long overdue change to improve efficiency and incentivize program integrity. Improper payment rates are high in many states (though they comprise both over-payments and under-payments, and error rates are different from fraud). Those that reduce errors enough won’t have to take on paying the benefits. And even opponents of the changes think lower error rates are a worthy goal. SNAP rolls often ebb and flow with the economy, and the recent drop could reflect the job market pulling people out of need — or the removal of people who shouldn’t have been getting food stamps in the first place. “There needs to be some level of accountability,” the USDA official said. States with high error rates “need to start to have skin in the game.” But at a time when many households are already squeezed by inflation, the SNAP changes have correlated with higher numbers of Americans turning to charities to ward off hunger. The surge in people losing food aid came more quickly than expected. The unemployment rate hasn’t meaningfully changed. And the vast majority of large food banks in a recent NBC survey said they were grappling with higher demand, in part due to food stamp changes. Another rule kicking in the day after the midterms could lead to many retailers being bumped out of SNAP as places where low-income people can use their benefits. For state governments, a set of sweeping operational changes are now underway to conform to new policy demands, often requiring more money or staffing at already under-resourced offices. And the budgetary stakes to get error rates lower are sky-high. “It’s a really complicated, nuanced and confusing time for states who are trying to administer SNAP,” said Lauren Kallins, a senior legislative director at the nonpartisan National Conference of State Legislatures, which has advocated for a delay in the benefits costs shift.

Erin Doherty Politico 1 h ago fresh drop

David Plouffe warns Dems: Don’t take North Carolina for granted

National Democrats are increasingly shifting their attention away from North Carolina’s Senate race as polls show former Gov. Roy Cooper ahead, eyeing once long-shot races as possible pickups. But a veteran Democratic strategist who helped deliver the party’s last presidential victory in the state is urging donors not to take a win for granted. David Plouffe, who managed behind Barack Obama’s narrow 2008 victory in North Carolina, urged Democratic donors and supporters not to grow complacent in the final weeks of Roy Cooper’s Senate campaign, according to audio obtained by POLITICO. “I think that this race ... has I think been the best run race in the country,” Plouffe said on the call. “But that doesn't mean that we can rest easy.” He warned about North Carolina’s relatively fixed partisan makeup as a purple state, making it difficult for a candidate to dramatically expand their base of support. “There's certain states that elections happen within a bound, and this one will be that way as well,” he said. In public polling, Cooper leads Republican Michael Whatley, who has struggled to boost his name recognition against the much better-known former governor. And as Democrats grow increasingly bullish on their candidate’s chances of flipping the seat — one of four pickups they need to take control of the Senate — national groups have begun shifting their money and attention to other contests, including most recently to Kansas . But Plouffe said North Carolina needs to remain a priority. “We have to win the ones we have to win,” he said on the call to Cooper’s finance committee. Just days before Plouffe’s remarks, Senate Democrats’ top super PAC pulled back some of its spending in North Carolina, following a much bigger retreat by Republicans’ top super PAC in the state. Plouffe cautioned that North Carolina has historically been a tough state for Democrats at the federal level, especially in recent years. The party hasn’t won a Senate race there since 2008, when Obama became the last Democratic presidential candidate to carry the state, winning by fewer than 15,000 votes. He lost the state in 2012. “Even though we carried the electoral votes back then, we only did so by I think 14,000 votes. So it was our narrowest victory,” Plouffe said. “And in 2012, we tried to win North Carolina again with the help of so many people on this phone, and we just couldn't get it done. And that tells you how difficult the state is.” Plouffe also cast the stakes of Cooper’s race as extending beyond November, arguing that a Cooper victory could provide a blueprint for the party’s eventual 2028 presidential nominee. “Democrats need to compete and win in North Carolina in 28,” he said. “And it's one thing to look how a governor can win a state. The best route, the best scout that you receive, is how someone in a federal race won in a tough state, and that can show you the way.”

Connor Greene TIME 3 h ago fresh drop

Are Firing Squad Executions Seeing a Revival in the U.S.?

The United States Disciplinary Barracks, where Nidal Malik Hasan is being held on death row, is seen in Fort Leavenworth. Hasan, the U.S. Army Major who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others during a mass shooting at Fort Hood in 2009, has been approved by President Donald Trump for execution by military firing squad. —Paul Hennessy—SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images Lethal injection has long been the prevailing method for carrying out the death penalty in the U.S. But supply-chain issues and a series of high-profile botched executions are increasingly causing officials around the country to weigh alternative options —including one that, until recently, had been all but entirely left in the past . Following the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee last week—the second botched execution in the state this year using lethal injection—several Tennessee lawmakers have publicly called for the state to turn to other methods. “If we’re having this much trouble with this particular means of execution, we need to take it off the table and go to something that’s far more reliable and predictable,” Tennessee Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson said while speaking on a local radio show on Monday. Republican Rep. Tim Burchett, who represents Tennessee's second congressional district in the House, similarly told local station WVLT last Friday that Tennessee should abandon lethal injection in favor of other methods that have “very little room for mistakes.” Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton told The Associated Press in an interview published on Monday that “I don’t think there’s any method that’s off the table at this point.” Among the potential alternatives named by both Johnson and Burchett was execution by firing squad. The method has been used exceedingly rarely in the U.S.: between 1976 and 2024, just three people were put to death by firing squad in the country, all of them in Utah. But the Tennessee lawmakers aren’t the only ones who have recently suggested reviving the practice—and some state officials and President Donald Trump have already made moves to do just that. Trump on Monday approved the U.S. Army’s first execution of a soldier via firing squad since World War II, greenlighting the use of the method to put to death Nidal Hasan, a former U.S. Army major and psychiatrist who was convicted of killing 13 people in a mass shooting at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, following a recommendation by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Hasan’s execution is scheduled to take place on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood and, Hegseth has announced, to be livestreamed . The approval comes months after Trump authorized the use of firing squads in federal executions in April. Both South Carolina and Idaho have also taken steps in recent months to either enable the use of firing squad executions or to carry them out. Last year, in the wake of a failed 2024 execution attempt using lethal injection in the state, South Carolina put three people to death by firing squad—doubling the number of such executions that had been carried out in the entire U.S. over the prior half-century. Idaho, meanwhile, enacted a law earlier this year that established the firing squad as the state’s primary method for carrying out the death penalty. That move, too, followed a high-profile botched execution via lethal injection in the state in 2024. How does a firing squad execution work? The specific procedure for execution by firing squad varies across different states, but the general method remains the same, according to Austin Sarat, a professor of law and political science at Amherst College and the author of Gruesome Spectacles: Botched Executions and America’s Death Penalty, . He explains that traditionally, a person is strapped to a chair, a hood is placed over their head and a target is put on their heart, to highlight where the shooters should aim. Then, between three and five people with high-powered rifles will fire at the target. In some states, one rifle will be loaded with a blank bullet, so that the shooters do not know who fired the fatal shots. “When the signal is given, they shoot into the heart of the condemned,” Sarat says. Which states allow execution by firing squad? Firing squad executions are currently permitted in just five states: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Utah. Idaho, under its recently enacted law, is the only state that uses the firing squad as its default method. The other states have designated execution by firing squad to be used as a fallback method if they are unable to carry out the death penalty by lethal injection, or as one of several methods that can be chosen by either corrections officials or inmates themselves to perform an execution. Utah in 2015 designated the firing squad as the alternative method to turn to if the state cannot, for instance, obtain the necessary drugs to perform an execution by lethal injection. Oklahoma permitted firing squads in 2011 as a method of last resort. Mississippi in 2022 gave discretion to corrections officials to choose among four methods, including the firing squad. And in South Carolina, the firing squad has since 2021 been one of multiple methods that death row inmates can choose for their means of execution, along with electrocution and lethal injection. If they do not choose a method, electrocution is used. Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, a non-profit organization that provides analysis and research on capital punishment, tells TIME that at least one inmate appears to have opted for the firing squad in the state last year due to a lack of information provided regarding what other forms of capital punishment entail. “Prisoners who asked for information about the other two methods of execution, namely the electric chair and lethal injection, were not given complete answers to understand how those methods would be used, and so at least in one of those cases, the prisoners felt like the firing squad was the only method of execution they knew enough about to choose,” Maher says. Lethal injection issues prompt a search for solutions Oklahoma became the first state to authorize lethal injection in 1977, as it sought more humane methods for capital punishment. From the late 1970s on, lethal injection was performed in Oklahoma and, later, other states using a three-drug protocol, explains Richard Levy, an anesthesiologist at Columbia University: one drug, sodium thiopental, to induce unconsciousness; a second paralytic drug to stop breathing; and potassium chloride to stop the heart from beating. In 2011, the company which manufactured sodium thiopental, Hospira, stopped manufacturing the drug, leaving states to revise their protocols for lethal injection. “Each state basically has adopted some variation on the theme,” Levy says in reference to the original three-drug protocol. He explains that the majority of states have since “gone to a single-drug approach,” a method he describes as “flawed and problematic.” Many states use a single dose of pentobarbital, which depresses the central nervous system. Levy explains that compared to thiopentol, pentobarbital doesn’t as effectively induce unconsciousness, “and probably doesn't reliably stop one from breathing.” Pike was given two doses of pentobarbital in her failed execution attempt before she was hospitalized; she complained that her arms were burning as the pentobarbital was administered, after several needles were unsuccessfully used to access a vein. Following the botched attempt, her lawyers believed she was brain dead on Monday, before she woke up on Tuesday. As of Thursday, Pike was “up and walking,” according to her lawyer. States have also struggled to obtain lethal injection drugs as a result of pharmaceutical companies’ opposition to supplying their products for executions. As a result, many states have substituted different drugs or opted for alternative execution methods. In South Carolina for instance, the state was unable to carry out executions for more than a decade after struggling to obtain lethal injection drugs, until 2021, when the state authorized firing squads and made electrocution its default method. In 2023, the governor’s office revealed that it had reached out to more than 1,300 contacts for execution drugs before finally obtaining pentobarbital. The state then resumed executions by lethal injection, but in March of 2025, a death row inmate chose to be executed by firing squad over fears of prolonged suffering related to lethal injection, becoming the first person to be executed by a firing squad in the state’s history. After it was unable to obtain sodium thiopental or pentobarbital, Oklahoma in 2014 switched to using midazolam , which has since been used in multiple executions that were considered botched. One Oklahoma execution using midazolam that year lasted 45 minutes. Republican Utah state Rep. Paul Ray, who sponsored the bill that reinstated firing squads in his state, cited difficulty obtaining the necessary drugs as a reason for the move when speaking with The Los Angeles Times in 2015. “We found out last year that there we had no ability to purchase more drugs. So looking down the road, we had to come up with a backup plan,” Ray told the outlet. “We decided to make it automatic to go to the firing squad.” Federal officials have given voice to similar reasoning. Before Trump authorized the use of firing squads for federal executions, the Department of Justice released a report in April which said that switching to “manners of execution that are currently provided for by the law of certain states … will help ensure the Department is prepared to carry out lawful executions even if a specific drug is unavailable.” The report also acknowledged “supply chain challenges that limit the availability of lethal injection drugs.” As those issues have complicated efforts to carry out lethal injection executions in recent years, botched attempts like the one in Pike’s case have also contributed to officials’ decisions to shift toward alternative methods. Lethal injection, by far the most common method of the death penalty in the U.S, also comes with the highest rate of botched attempts, according to research performed by Sarat, the Amherst college professor. In one comprehensive study that examined executions between 1890 and 2010, Sarat found that just over 7% of executions by lethal injection were botched. In a subsequent study looking at executions performed between 2010 and 2020, he found that the rate was over 8%. “It is certain. It is quick. And it brings justice for the victims and their families in a more expeditious manner than other types,” said Idaho state Rep. Bruce Skaug, who sponsored the bill that established the firing squad as the state’s default method. Historically, in the scant instances when firing squad executions have been carried out in the U.S, they’ve rarely—if ever—been botched, according to Sarat’s study. Out of 34 executions by firing squad between 1890 and 2010, he found, not one went significantly awry. In one of the three firing squad executions performed in South Carolina last year, though, an autopsy report concluded that the firing squad missed the heart of the victim, indicating that he did not immediately die and may have endured suffering. Sarat argues that firing squads, though involved in far fewer botched executions, remain a “brutal” form of capital punishment that “was abandoned because it didn't meet the evolving standards of decency of the society.” “Since the end of the 19th century, the United States has been on a quest to find a method of execution that would be safe, reliable, and humane. The firing squad has never played a big role in that story,” Sarat tells TIME. “It hasn't played a big role in that story because it is a brutal way to kill someone, and its brutality is very obvious.” Other forms of capital punishment have also received consideration in recent years in the search for potential alternatives to lethal injection. The DOJ’s report from April directed federal prisons to expand their methods of execution to include, along with firing squads, gas asphyxiation and electrocution. Alabama in 2024 became the first state to execute a death row inmate using nitrogen gas, and four other states have adopted the practice since. In 2025, 19 bills in 14 states were introduced to alter or augment execution methods, according to the Death Penalty Information Center . Despite the moves to revive largely bygone execution methods or implement new ones, however, Sarat emphasizes that capital punishment is overall trending down. The death penalty is currently outlawed in 23 states, while 10 others have not carried out an execution in the last decade, according to the Death Penalty Information Center . An additional four states have not had an execution in the last five years. “The United States is on the road to abolition … The death penalty is dying,” Sarat says. “I don't think that either what Trump has done about the firing squad or Christa Pike's failed execution, in and of itself, is going to make a huge dent in America's death penalty.”

The data on the impact of those first months on a child’s brain suggest we have been treating a critical developmental window like a scheduling inconvenience. Employers and employees basically agree on a need to strive for work-life balance. And while the gender equity argument is used to both advance and stymie conversations about paternity leave, it is more than a values fight. It turns out that paternity leave and a father’s engagement during infancy is associated with better cognitive, social, and emotional regulation outcomes for the child that can be measured. In a review of existing fatherhood research, Sarah Schoppe-Sullivan, a researcher at the Ohio State University, highlighted better peer relationships, higher intelligence test scores, greater math and language readiness and development, and more secure attachment formation among children who experience positive and sustained father involvement compared to those who don’t. Though these trends are correlational, these father-involvement gains show up on report cards as early as preschool and can continue into adulthood. One possible avenue through which these benefits pass from father to child is the quality of play. Canadian researcher Daniel Paquette observed that father’s play often includes excitement, surprise, awe, and temporary shock and disruption for children, and this kind of interaction is the foundation for crucial developmental skills like risk-taking , personal efficacy , and self-advocacy. Children who have more consistent positive engagement with their fathers have better outcomes across some of the main child mental-health domains, including anxiety, depression, and behavioral problems. Paternity leave creates space for and helps develop active involvement like physical play, showing up to school events, and careful listening to a child, and these are connected to healthy child development . Secure attachment, more prosocial sibling interactions, and better social competence result in other benefits, like self-regulation. This is a hallmark indicator of school readiness and success, and here, too, father engagement pays dividends. What looks like fathers rough-housing, developmentally speaking, is training for children to build capacity for self-regulation, managing arousal, and controlling impulses and emotions in real time . Early literacy and home-visiting programs like Head Start are widely celebrated for similar child development outcomes, but father engagement has additional social, developmental, and familial benefits including improved parenting relationships. Moreover, other countries have found success in persuading more fathers to take paid paternity leave after shifting to a “use-it-or-lose-it” policy , by which a portion of paid parental leave is reserved exclusively for fathers and is non-transferable to the mother. Compared to earlier trends dating back to the early 2000s, paid paternal leave uptake has steadily increased; in Iceland, just 15% of fathers took leave in 1998, while more than over 80% did in 2002 . Spain recorded a 400% increase from 2000 to 2007 . Also in 2007, after Germany replaced their flat-rate leave pay with an income-based benefit (i.e., 67% of net earnings) and reserved two “use-it-or-lose-it” months for fathers, uptake of parental leave increased from 3.5% in 2006 to 24.8% in 2021. The U.S. is lagging far behind in this area. Where paternity leave does exist, it is often unpaid and unguaranteed, and mothers for instance, cannot transfer a portion of their allotted maternity leave to the father to allow him to take extra time off. This means that many fathers do not use this critical child development and family resource. Most new fathers are back at their desk within a week of their child’s birth, right as the research suggests their presence does some of its most consequential work. We can increase the uptake of this resource with federal paid leave legislation, which will improve access to leave for all fathers. This would have the potential to lead to widespread positive cognitive, academic, and emotional development of children. Employers need not wait on legislation. They can apply the “use-it-or-lose” approach at their companies in the best interest of their employees. Fathers’ access to and use of paternity leave is not a question of available employment benefits. It is a developmental one, and we already know how to answer development questions. We don’t treat prenatal care as a “nice perk.” We should not be treating the first months of a father’s presence like that, either.
